title: Children Act 1989 and 2004: paramountcy, children in need, s47 and s11 duties
blurb: Use the Children Act 1989 and 2004 to decide whether a child is in need, at risk of significant harm, and what your trust must do.
question: Kofi, 3, attends the children's emergency department with a spiral fracture of the femur. His mother says he fell off the sofa, but he is not yet walking steadily. Under which part of the Children Act 1989 would children's social care act on the nurse's referral, and on what test?

teach.body: The Children Act 1989 is the backbone of child law in England and Wales: it defines a child (anyone under 18, s105), parental responsibility, children in need (s17) and the local authority's duty to investigate significant harm (s47). The Children Act 2004 built the multi-agency system around it: the duty on NHS bodies and others to safeguard (s11) and the three safeguarding partners. In plain English: 1989 says what the child is owed; 2004 says how agencies must organise to deliver it.
teach.cite: Children Act 1989 ss1, 17, 47, 105; Children Act 2004 ss10, 11

items.label: the child's welfare is the court's paramount consideration
duty to children in need, including every disabled child
enquiries on reasonable cause to suspect significant harm

teach.caption: Reaching 16, living independently, being in further education, the armed forces, hospital or custody does not change a child's status or protection (Working Together 2026 glossary).

teach.h: Paramountcy, no delay, the welfare checklist
teach.body: When a court decides any question about a child's upbringing, the child's welfare is its paramount consideration (s1(1)): it outweighs the wishes of parents. Delay is likely to prejudice the child's welfare (s1(2)), and the court makes no order unless doing so is better for the child than not (s1(5)). In contested cases it applies the s1(3) welfare checklist, starting with the child's own wishes and feelings in the light of age and understanding.

head: s1(3)
The court considers...
rows: The child's wishes and feelings, in light of age and understanding
Likely effect of any change in circumstances
Harm suffered or at risk of
How capable each parent (or other person) is of meeting needs
The range of powers available to the court
teach.caption: Nurses often hold the evidence for (a), (b) and (e): record the child's own words and observed needs accurately.

teach.h: Child in need (s17) vs significant harm (s47)

rows.label: Test
values: Reasonable cause to suspect significant harm

teach.caption: s17(10): in need if unlikely to achieve a reasonable standard of health or development, or likely to be significantly impaired, without services, or disabled.

teach.h: Which route does a concern take?

root.label: Concern about a child
root.sub: Share with safeguarding lead; refer to children's social care

teach.caption: Social care decides next steps within one working day of a referral (Working Together 2026 para 167).

teach.h: Significant harm and the s31 threshold
teach.body: 'Harm' means ill-treatment or impairment of health or development, including impairment from seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another (s31(9)). A court can make a care or supervision order only if the child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm attributable to care below what a reasonable parent would give, or to being beyond parental control (s31(2)). Nurses do not have to prove harm: s47 begins on reasonable cause to suspect it.

Effect for nurses
rows: Agencies cooperate to improve children's well-being
NHS trusts, FTs, ICBs, police must arrange to safeguard

Duty to share safeguarding information (30 Sept 2026)
teach.caption: s11(2): functions discharged 'having regard to the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children', including services they contract out.

teach.h: Applying it: Kofi in the ED
teach.body: A femoral fracture in a child who cannot walk steadily, with an implausible explanation, gives reasonable cause to suspect significant harm. The nurse ensures treatment, records the account verbatim, informs the named nurse or safeguarding lead and makes a referral to children's social care. Social care decides next steps within one working day; a strategy discussion (social care, police, health) can start s47 enquiries. The trust's s11 duty is why the ED has a safeguarding policy and a named nurse.

teach.text: s17 and s47 are not two levels of the same test. s17 is about needing services (and covers every disabled child) and runs with the family's agreement; s47 starts on 'reasonable cause to suspect' significant harm, actual or likely, and no proof or parental consent is needed. Paramountcy (s1) binds the court; it is not the threshold for a referral.

items: Child = under 18 (s105), whatever their living or work situation.
s1: welfare paramount for the court; delay is likely to prejudice welfare; s1(3) checklist starts with the child's wishes and feelings.
s17: child in need, including every disabled child: assessment and support.
s47: reasonable cause to suspect significant harm, actual or likely: enquiries.
s31: care order threshold; harm includes seeing or hearing ill-treatment of another.
CA 2004 s11: NHS trusts, FTs and ICBs must arrange their functions to safeguard children; three safeguarding partners lead local arrangements.

summary: You can now tell a child in need (s17) from a child at risk of significant harm (s47), explain paramountcy and the welfare checklist, and describe the s11 duty on NHS bodies. You can also apply the s31 meaning of harm, including harm from witnessing ill-treatment.

A.q: Tomás, 17, has left home and lives in a hostel while working full time. He is admitted after an assault. A colleague says the Children Act 1989 safeguarding duties no longer apply to him. Which response is accurate?
options: They apply until his 16th birthday if he is employed
They apply, because the Act treats anyone under 18 as a child
They apply once a court has made an order about him
They apply while his parents continue to hold parental responsibility
A.why: Section 105 defines a child as a person under 18, with no exception for employment. Working Together 2026 (glossary) adds that reaching 16 or living independently does not change a child's status or entitlement to protection.

whyNot.0: There is no employment cut-off at 16 in the definition of a child.
whyNot.2: The definition of a child does not depend on any court order.
whyNot.3: Protection under the Act does not depend on who holds parental responsibility.

A.q: Hana, 6, has severe cerebral palsy. Her parents are coping but would like respite care and equipment. A student asks how the Children Act 1989 classifies her. Which answer is correct?
options: A child in need under section 17, because she is disabled
A child at risk under section 47, because she is disabled
A looked after child under section 20, because she needs care
A child in need under section 17 once a parent is struggling
A.why: s17(10)(c) makes every disabled child a child in need, so the local authority can assess and provide services such as short breaks.

whyNot.1: s47 needs reasonable cause to suspect significant harm; disability alone is not that.
whyNot.2: Section 20 is accommodation; nothing suggests Hana needs to be accommodated.
whyNot.3: Disability is enough on its own; parents do not first have to be struggling.

A.q: What test must be met before a local authority makes enquiries under section 47 of the Children Act 1989?
options: Proof on the balance of probabilities that the child is being harmed
Parental agreement that an assessment of the family is needed
Reasonable cause to suspect actual or likely significant harm
A finding by a court that the child is beyond parental control
A.why: s47(1)(b) is triggered by reasonable cause to suspect significant harm, actual or likely. No proof is needed.

whyNot.0: Proof is the court's job later; s47 enquiries start on suspicion.
whyNot.1: s47 enquiries do not depend on parental agreement.
whyNot.3: 'Beyond parental control' is part of the s31 care order threshold, not the trigger for s47.

B.q: A family court is deciding where Leila, 9, should live after her parents separate. Her father argues that his wishes as a parent should carry most weight. What principle will the court apply?
options: The parents' agreed wishes are its first consideration
Leila's wishes are decisive once she is aged nine or over
The parent with parental responsibility has the final say
Leila's welfare is the court's paramount consideration
B.why: s1(1): when a court determines any question about a child's upbringing, the child's welfare is paramount. Leila's wishes are weighed in the light of her age and understanding within the s1(3) checklist.

whyNot.0: Parents' wishes are relevant but do not outrank the child's welfare.
whyNot.1: The child's wishes are one checklist factor, not decisive at a set age.
whyNot.2: Both parents may hold parental responsibility; the court decides on welfare.

B.q: Ruby, 7, is admitted with asthma. She tells the nurse she covers her ears when her stepfather hits her mother. She has no injuries. How does the Children Act 1989 treat this?
options: It is not harm under the Act unless Ruby herself is struck
It can be harm, as impairment from seeing or hearing ill-treatment counts
It is a matter for adult safeguarding services, as the abuse is between adults
It can be harm once a court has convicted the stepfather
B.why: s31(9) defines harm to include impairment suffered from seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another, so Ruby's welfare is directly engaged and a referral is needed.

whyNot.0: The statutory definition expressly includes harm from witnessing ill-treatment.
whyNot.2: Adult services may help her mother, but Ruby's own safety is a children's safeguarding issue.
whyNot.3: No conviction is needed for harm to exist or for a referral to be made.

B.q: A ward manager asks why the Children Act 2004 obliges an NHS foundation trust to have safeguarding policies and named professionals. Which section creates that duty?
options: Section 47, the duty to make child protection enquiries
Section 17, the duty to support children in need
Section 11, the duty to make safeguarding arrangements
Section 1, the duty to treat welfare as paramount
B.why: CA 2004 s11 lists NHS trusts, foundation trusts and ICBs, which must make arrangements so their functions are discharged having regard to the need to safeguard and promote children's welfare.

whyNot.0: s47 is a 1989 Act duty on the local authority, not on NHS trusts.
whyNot.1: s17 is a local authority duty to children in need.
whyNot.3: s1 governs court decisions about a child's upbringing.

C.q: A health visitor refers Eliza, 2, to children's social care because of unexplained bruising to both ears. By the end of the next working day she has heard nothing. What should she expect under Working Together 2026, and what should she do?
options: A decision on next steps within 45 working days; wait for the assessment
An initial conference within 15 working days; prepare a written report
No contact until s47 ends; continue her routine visiting plan
A decision within one working day; follow it up and escalate
C.why: Working Together 2026 para 167: within one working day social care should acknowledge the referral and a manager should decide next steps. If the referrer hears nothing she follows up, using local escalation procedures if needed.

whyNot.0: 45 working days is the maximum for completing an assessment, not for deciding next steps.
whyNot.1: 15 working days runs from the strategy discussion to the initial conference.
whyNot.2: Waiting silently leaves Eliza unprotected; the referrer should follow up.

C.q: Arlo, 4, has autism and his parents ask for support at home. The nurse also notes he is losing weight and has missed three hospital appointments. Which statement best describes the legal position?
options: He is a child in need, and the new concerns may also justify a s47 referral
He is a child in need, so a s47 referral is excluded while s17 support continues
He is outside s17 because his parents are asking for help voluntarily
He is outside s47 until a court finds that his care is unreasonable
C.why: Arlo's disability makes him a child in need (s17), but s17 status does not prevent s47 enquiries. Weight loss and missed appointments may give reasonable cause to suspect neglect, so the nurse shares this with the safeguarding lead and social care.

whyNot.1: A child can move from s17 to s47 at any point if significant harm is suspected.
whyNot.2: s17 support is normally provided by agreement; asking for help does not exclude it.
whyNot.3: No court finding is needed; s47 starts on reasonable cause to suspect.

C.q: During a case review, a manager suggests delaying a decision about where Jayden, 18 months, should live until his father finishes a rehabilitation programme next year. Which Children Act 1989 principle is most directly in tension with this?
options: The no-order principle in section 1(5)
The welfare checklist factor on parental capability
The presumption that delay prejudices welfare
The duty to children in need in section 17
C.why: s1(2): any delay in determining a question about a child's upbringing is likely to prejudice the child's welfare. For an 18-month-old, a year is a long time.

whyNot.0: The no-order principle is about whether to make an order, not about timing.
whyNot.1: Parental capability is relevant, but the problem here is the delay itself.
whyNot.3: s17 concerns services for children in need, not the timing of decisions.

reteach.title: Two doors into children's social care
reteach.question: How do I know whether a concern is about 'need' or 'harm'?

blocks.body: Think of two doors. The s17 door is for children who need extra help to stay healthy or develop well, including every disabled child: the family works with services by agreement. The s47 door opens when there is reasonable cause to suspect a child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm: enquiries happen whether or not parents agree. You do not have to choose the door yourself: you share the concern and refer; social care decides within one working day.

steps.label: Share
steps.sub: Safeguarding lead; referral to social care

steps.label: Decide
steps.sub: Social care within one working day

blocks.text: Suspicion is enough for s47: the test is 'reasonable cause to suspect', not proof. Harm includes what a child sees or hears (s31(9)).

explain.body: In court decisions about a child's upbringing, the child's welfare is paramount (s1(1)). Delay is presumed harmful (s1(2)). The s1(3) checklist starts with the child's wishes and feelings in light of age and understanding.

test.q: Which factor comes first in the s1(3) welfare checklist?
options: The capability of each parent and other carers to meet the child's needs
The child's wishes and feelings in light of age and understanding
The range of powers available to the court
The child's age, sex and background
test.why: s1(3)(a) is the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the child, considered in the light of age and understanding.

whyNot.3: Age, sex and background are factor (d).

explain.body: A child is in need if unlikely to achieve or maintain a reasonable standard of health or development without services, if health or development is likely to be significantly impaired without them, or if the child is disabled (s17(10)).

children.edge: Health or development at risk without services
children.label: Yes

test.q: Which child automatically meets the s17 definition of a child in need?
options: A child whose parents are on a low income
A child who has been admitted to hospital
A child who has a significant disability
A child who has a parent in prison
test.why: s17(10)(c): a disabled child is a child in need. The others may be in need, but only if the health or development tests are met.

whyNot.0: Low income alone does not meet the definition.
whyNot.1: Admission to hospital alone does not meet the definition.
whyNot.3: A parent in prison may create need, but it is not an automatic category.

explain.body: The local authority must make enquiries where it has reasonable cause to suspect a child in its area is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm (s47(1)(b)). Harm includes ill-treatment and impairment of health or development, including from seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another (s31(9)).

test.q: Who must, as a minimum, take part in a strategy discussion about suspected significant harm?
options: Social care, health and police
Social care, the school and the GP
Health, police and the parents
Social care, police and the LADO
test.why: Working Together 2026: a local authority social worker, health practitioners and a police representative should, as a minimum, be involved.

whyNot.1: Education and the GP may join, but police are part of the minimum.
whyNot.2: Parents are not members of the strategy discussion.
whyNot.3: The LADO handles allegations against staff, not every strategy discussion.

explain.body: s11 lists bodies including NHS England, ICBs, NHS trusts, foundation trusts and police, which must make arrangements so their functions, and services they commission, are discharged having regard to the need to safeguard and promote children's welfare.

test.q: An NHS trust contracts a private provider to run its children's outpatient clinics. What does s11 require of the trust?
options: That the provider registers as a fourth safeguarding partner
That the provider makes s47 enquiries into concerns it identifies
That the trust's safeguarding duty ends where the provider's contract begins
That services it arranges are provided having regard to safeguarding
test.why: s11(2)(b): services provided by another person under the body's arrangements must also be provided having regard to the need to safeguard and promote children's welfare.

whyNot.0: The three safeguarding partners are the LA, the ICB and police.
whyNot.1: s47 enquiries are a local authority duty.
whyNot.2: s11(2)(b) extends the duty to commissioned services.
